newsitem.title: THAILAND: Floods may delay Thai sugar cane crush, hit output.
newsitem.headline: Floods may delay Thai sugar cane crush, hit output.

text.p: Floods in growing areas could delay Thai sugar cane crushing this year and output may drop below forecasts of more than 60 million tonnes, officials and industry sources said on Wednesday.
A tripartite board of government representatives, cane farmers and millers will hold a meeting on October 18 to review the situation before setting the seasonal crushing schedule, they told Reuters.

"Based on information we have received so far, it is almost impossible that the cane output will exceed 60 million tonnes," said Porntip Visarat from the Industry Ministry's Office of the Cane and Sugar Board.
"The flood could also delay the crushing schedule as farmers might not be able to transport cane to mills," she added.

There are 46 sugar mills in Thailand. The crushing season normally starts in early November, with mills in northeastern areas being the first to start. Sugar mills in the northern and central regions normally start crushing in December.
The initial proposed start-up date for crushing in the northeastern region is November 5.
Some millers said they were concerned about the amount of cane that would be available for crushing at their mills.

"Our mills were barely affected by the floods, thanks to the location. We are ready for crushing. But how badly the floods will affect cane cutting and transporting is a problem," said a mill official in northeastern region.
But some other millers said their factories had been hit by floods, especially their water treatment facilities. However, they said repairs would be completed in time for the crushing.
Others feared the floods could affect the sugar content in the cane and consequently reduce sugar output.
The extent of the flood damage to the 1996/97 (November-October) sugar cane crop is not clear. The agriculture ministry has yet to release its forecast revision.
The ministry's last forecast put sugar cane output at 62.42 million tonnes.
Despite continuing concerns over flood damage, cane farmers in some areas remain optimistic that the floods will have only a minimal effect on the crushing schedule.

"The water level has decreased in many areas. If it does not continue to rain, the cane in this area should be ready for crushing on schedule," said Somkuan Duangbuntao, an assistant manager of the sugar cane planters' association of Zone 7.
Zone 7 covers 193,861 hectares of cane growing areas in five central provinces.
